summary: A snapshot of the many RFCs that define and use IPsec and IKE, which come from numerous working groups, organized as a roadmap. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IPsec protects network traffic, and IKE is the protocol that agrees the keys it uses. Both have grown into families of dozens of RFCs written by different working groups. This RFC is a map of that family: it names the current documents, explains how they fit together, lists the cryptographic algorithms each one calls for, and sets out what changed between the older and the newer versions.

subtitle: A map of the many RFCs that define IP security and key exchange, and where the old and new versions differ.

tldr.problem: The RFCs that define and use IPsec and IKE come from many IETF working groups and have multiplied over the years, so it is hard to see which document is current, which is obsolete, and how the old and new versions of the protocols differ.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists and briefly describes the IPsec and IKE documents, groups them by role, and records the requirement level of every cryptographic algorithm for IKEv1, IKEv2, IPsec-v2 and IPsec-v3.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational snapshot that obsoletes RFC 2411. The requirement levels it records were current in February 2011, and the RFC says later documents may change them.

today: RFC 6071 was published in February 2011 as an Informational document and obsoletes RFC 2411, the earlier IP Security Document Roadmap. It has not been obsoleted or updated since. The algorithm requirement levels it records were current in February 2011, and the document itself notes that later RFCs may introduce new algorithms or change those levels.

sections.title: Why This Roadmap Exists
sections.content:
IPsec is a suite of protocols that provides security to Internet communications at the IP layer. Its most common use is a Virtual Private Network, either between two locations or between a remote user and an enterprise network, and it can also give end-to-end protection between two hosts. IKE is the key negotiation and management protocol most commonly used to provide dynamically negotiated and updated keying material for IPsec. Both work with IPv4 and IPv6.

Beyond the base documents, many RFCs reference, extend and sometimes alter the core specifications, and they come from many working groups: the original IPsec working group, its spin-offs, and other groups that use IPsec or IKE to protect their own traffic. This RFC is a snapshot of the IPsec- and IKE-related RFCs, with a brief description of each and background explaining the motivation behind the outgrowths and extensions. It obsoletes RFC 2411, the previous IP Security Document Roadmap, whose focus was the recommended contents of documents specifying additional encryption and authentication algorithms.

Each RFC listed carries a letter after its title showing its category in the RFC series: S for Standards Track, E for Experimental, B for Best Current Practice and I for Informational. The publication date is given as well.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec is the network security layer, and IKE is the protocol that sets up the keys it needs. Dozens of RFCs describe them. This document is a catalogue of those RFCs, so a reader can tell which one is current and what each one adds.

sections.title: How the IPsec Documents Fit Together
sections.content:
The main documents describing IPsec are divided into seven groups, and the RFC draws them as a diagram. At the top is an architecture document that covers the general concepts, the security requirements, the definitions and the mechanisms that define IPsec technology.

Below it sit two protocol documents. The Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) protocol document and the Authentication Header (AH) protocol document each cover a packet format and the general issues of their protocol. Under ESP there are three sets of algorithm documents. The encryption algorithm set, shown on the left, describes how various encryption algorithms are used for ESP. The combined algorithm set, in the middle, describes how combined mode algorithms give both encryption and integrity protection for ESP. The integrity-protection algorithm set, on the right, describes how integrity-protection algorithms are used for both ESP and AH.

At the bottom are the IKE documents, which describe the Standards Track key management schemes. The architecture document also introduces the components the rest of the documents use: the Security Association, a one-way agreement between two peers about which protections, algorithms, keys and traffic types apply; the Security Parameters Index, which together with the destination address and the protocol identifies a single association; the Security Association Database, each peer's own repository of associations; and the Security Policy Database, an ordered database saying which traffic is discarded, which is allowed without protection and which requires protection.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFCs stack up. One describes the overall design. Two describe the packet formats that carry the protection. Three sets of documents then say which encryption and integrity algorithms each format may use, and a further set describes IKE, which is what agrees the keys in the first place.

sections.title: Two Versions of IPsec
sections.content:
Two versions of IPsec can be found in implementations. The new IPsec, called IPsec-v3 in this document, obsoleted the old IPsec, called IPsec-v2, but IPsec-v2 is still commonly found in operational use. When this RFC uses the unqualified term IPsec it means both. An earlier version, defined in RFCs 1825 to 1829 and obsoleted by IPsec-v2, is not covered here.

IPsec-v3 was written with the lessons learned from running IPsec-v2 and its predecessor. The RFC lists what changed in the architecture document: more detailed descriptions of IPsec processing for both unicast and multicast traffic and of the interactions among the databases; more flexible Security Policy Database selectors, including ranges of values and ICMP message types; a decorrelated, order-independent Security Association Database in place of the former ordered one; extended sequence numbers; and mandatory algorithms defined in a standalone document. How a unicast association is identified also changed. In IPsec-v2 a Security Association is uniquely identified by the Security Parameters Index together with the protocol and the destination address. In IPsec-v3 a unicast association is identified by the index and, optionally, the protocol, while a multicast association is identified by the index and the destination address and, optionally, the source address. IPsec-v3 also adds a fourth database, the Peer Authorization Database, which holds the information needed to authenticate a peer and links IPsec to the key management protocol.

Two changes affect the two protocol documents. Combined mode algorithms were added to ESP, which required changes to the packet format and to processing. NULL authentication, mandatory in ESP-v2, is optional in ESP-v3. The Authentication Header is mandatory to implement in IPsec-v2 and optional in IPsec-v3.
sections.plainLanguage: The older version of IPsec is still in use, so both are described. The newer one keeps the same basic pieces but changes how a protected flow is identified, adds a database for peer identity, allows algorithms that do both encryption and integrity checking in one step, and makes the Authentication Header optional rather than required.

sections.title: Two Versions of IKE
sections.content:
IKE also has two versions in use. IKEv2 obsoleted IKEv1, but IKEv1 is still commonly found in operational use, and when this RFC uses the unqualified term IKE it means both. IKEv2 grew out of the same lessons learned about the barriers to deployment, the scenarios where IKE works best and the requirements needed to use it with other protocols. Its documentation also replaced several separate and at times contradictory documents with a single document, and clarified details that were underspecified or ambiguous in IKEv1.

The RFC first settles the terminology. When an IKE negotiation completes, the peers have established two pairs of one-way Security Associations. Because IKE always negotiates pairs, the term Security Association generally refers to a pair. The first, the IKE SA, protects IKE traffic. The second provides IPsec protection to data traffic between the peers, and is called the IPsec SA in IKEv1 and variously a CHILD_SA, a child SA or an IPsec SA in the IKEv2 RFCs. Because IKEv1 consists of two sequential negotiations, called phases, the IKE SA is also called a Phase 1 SA and the IPsec SA a Phase 2 SA.

The list of changes is short. IKEv2 replaced multiple alternate exchange types with a single, shorter exchange, and streamlined the negotiation format to avoid combinatorial bloat when several proposals are on the table. It protects the responder from committing significant resources until the initiator's existence and identity are confirmed. Every request now expects a response. Protection of IKE messages is based on ESP rather than on a method unique to IKE. It adds traffic selectors, distinct from peer identities and more flexible, and supports EAP-based authentication methods and asymmetric authentication, so that the initiator and the responder may use different authentication methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The newer key exchange, IKEv2, replaced a tangle of separate documents with one and changed the exchange itself: one message flow instead of several, a response expected for every request, and the responder no longer commits resources before the other side proves who it is. The older IKEv1 remains in wide use, so the RFC describes both.

sections.title: Cryptographic Algorithms and Requirement Levels
sections.content:
Two basic requirements must be met before an algorithm can be used within IKE or IPsec: it must have one or more IANA values assigned, and there must be an RFC that describes how to use it within the relevant protocol. For each such RFC the roadmap classifies the requirement level for IKEv1, IKEv2, IPsec-v2 and IPsec-v3 as MUST, SHOULD or MAY, as the qualified forms SHOULD+, SHOULD- or MUST-, or as optional, undefined or not applicable.

The RFC explains what the three non-standard labels mean. A designation of optional means the algorithm meets the two basic requirements but its use is not specifically recommended for that protocol. Undefined means one of the basic requirements is not met, either because there is no relevant IANA number or because no RFC says how to use it in that protocol. Not applicable means that using the algorithm is inappropriate in the context, as with NULL encryption for IKE, which always requires encryption, or with combined mode algorithms, a new feature in IPsec-v3, used with IPsec-v2.

The requirements are split by role. An algorithm recommended for IKEv1 or IKEv2 either protects the traffic of the IKE SA, in the case of encryption and integrity-protection algorithms, or generates keying material, in the case of Diffie-Hellman groups and pseudorandom functions. An algorithm recommended for IPsec protects the traffic of the IPsec SA, and IKE is able to negotiate its use for that purpose. Appendix A collects the levels in one table. The RFC notes that the levels are current as of February 2011, that later RFCs may introduce new algorithms or upgrade or downgrade the levels of current ones, and that this document does not define requirement levels of its own but only restates those found in the IKE and IPsec RFCs, with any conflict resolved in favour of the other RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each algorithm gets a strength label for each of the four protocol versions, and Appendix A lists them all. The label says whether an implementation must support the algorithm, should support it, or may ignore it. The RFC is a mirror of labels set elsewhere, so if a label here disagrees with the RFC that set it, the other RFC wins.

sections.title: Outgrowths and Other Users of IPsec
sections.content:
Operational experience with IPsec produced a set of outgrowths, which the RFC groups in its own section. They include IPsec policy mechanisms, IPsec MIBs for management, payload compression through IPComp, extensions that allow further peer authentication methods such as Better-Than-Nothing Security, Kerberized Internet Negotiation of Keys and the IPSECKEY resource record, and extra capabilities for VPN clients collected under IPsec Secure Remote Access. Not all of them were taken up. The IPsec policy work aimed at letting two parties with no common trust anchor negotiate a protected connection, but the proposed solutions for gateway discovery and policy negotiation proved too complex and fragile without prior knowledge, and the RFC says the IPsec configuration policy document has not been widely adopted.

Multicast needed its own treatment, because classical IPsec associations give point-to-point protection and the security that IPsec's cryptographic algorithms provide does not apply when the association is one-to-many or many-to-many. The Multicast Security working group defined alternatives to IKE and extensions to IPsec for multicast traffic, and the RFC lists the multicast security architecture, the multicast extensions to the IPsec architecture, the Group Domain of Interpretation, the group key management architecture and the use of RSA with SHA-1 signatures.

Finally, a long section lists other protocols that use IPsec or IKE to protect some or all of their communications, because IPsec is general purpose and its features do not always give the granularity another protocol needs. The list covers Mobile IP in both versions, OSPFv3, the Host Identity Protocol, SCTP, Robust Header Compression, BGP, benchmarking, Network Address Translators, the Session Initiation Protocol and the CALIPSO sensitivity label option. A shorter section covers protocols that protect their traffic another way but borrow IKEv2 for key negotiation: the Extensible Authentication Protocol method EAP-IKEv2, Fibre Channel, which adapted IKEv2 so that a mistaken use over the wrong network fails at negotiation, and GigaBeam radio link encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of what grew around IPsec was adopted and some was not. The RFC sorts the field into pieces that extend IPsec itself, the separate work needed for multicast, and the many other protocols that borrow IPsec or IKE to protect their own traffic.
